title: Why Your Front-Load Washer Smells Musty or Moldy (and How to Fix It for Good)
question: My front-load washer smells musty and moldy even after I run it — why does it stink, and how do I actually clean it out and keep the smell from coming back?
summary: The smell is almost never the clothes — it's biofilm: a slimy mix of mold, bacteria, and detergent scum growing in the rubber door gasket, the detergent drawer, and the drain filter. The thing most people get wrong is thinking a single bleach "clean cycle" will fix it. It won't, because the worst gunk sits in gasket folds and drawer corners the water never reaches. You have to physically scrub those spots AND change the habits that feed the mold: too much HE detergent or fabric softener, and shutting the door and drawer between washes so the drum stays damp.

commonCauses.cause: Biofilm and mold trapped in the folds of the rubber door gasket (the flexible boot around the door)
commonCauses.quickCheck: Peel back the rubber gasket lip and shine a flashlight into the folds; black or gray slime, hair, and a sour smell there confirm it.

commonCauses.cause: Mold and residue built up in the detergent/softener drawer and the cavity it slides into
commonCauses.quickCheck: Slide the drawer all the way out and look at the fabric-softener compartment and the roof of the empty slot for pink, black, or gray mold and sludge.

commonCauses.cause: Overdosing detergent or regularly using liquid fabric softener, which leaves a film the mold feeds on
commonCauses.quickCheck: Check whether you fill past the HE line or add softener most loads; leftover suds or a slimy film in the drum after a cycle means residue is building up.

commonCauses.cause: Keeping the door and detergent drawer closed between washes, so the drum stays warm and damp
commonCauses.quickCheck: If you shut the door right after unloading, feel inside an hour later — a drum that stays wet and never dries out is a breeding ground.

commonCauses.cause: Clogged drain pump filter or sump holding a pocket of dirty, standing water
commonCauses.quickCheck: Open the small access panel at the lower front, unscrew the filter over a towel, and check the water that drains out — foul-smelling water and trapped lint/coins point to the sump as the source.

fixes: Deep-clean the door gasket first. Put on rubber gloves, peel back each fold of the rubber boot, and pull out hair, lint, and gunk. Wipe every fold with a cloth dipped in a cleaning solution — use ONE of the following, never mixed: diluted chlorine bleach (about 3/4 cup bleach per gallon of water) OR a washer-safe cleaner. Note that LG and Samsung caution against vinegar on seals, so favor bleach or a dedicated washer cleaner for the rubber.

Remove and scrub the detergent drawer. Pull it fully out (most have a small release tab or push-point in the middle), then scrub the drawer and especially the softener cup with warm soapy water and an old toothbrush. Reach up into the empty cavity and clean the underside of the dispenser roof and the nozzle where mold hides; a cotton swab helps. Rinse, dry, and slide it back in.

Run the tub-clean cycle empty. Add EITHER a washing-machine cleaner tablet (such as Affresh or Tide Washing Machine Cleaner) OR about 1 cup of chlorine bleach directly in the drum — never both in the same cycle, and no detergent and no clothes — then run the 'Tub Clean'/'Self Clean' cycle, or the hottest, longest normal cycle if yours has none. If you just bleached the gasket, either use bleach again here or run an extra rinse before switching to an oxygen-based tablet, so cleaners don't mix in the drum.
Run one extra rinse-and-spin afterward to flush out loosened residue and any leftover bleach.

Clean the drain pump filter. Unplug the washer first (or switch off its breaker). If you just ran a hot cycle, wait for any trapped water to cool so it can't scald you. Open the small panel at the lower front, and lay down towels with a shallow pan — water will spill. Slowly unscrew the filter, let it drain in stages, clear out lint, coins, and slime, rinse it under the tap, then screw it back in snugly. Check your owner's manual for the exact location and steps.
Wipe the door glass and gasket dry, and towel out any water pooled in the bottom fold of the boot.

Change the habit that feeds the mold: leave the door propped open and pull the detergent drawer out an inch or two between washes so the inside air-dries. If you have small kids or pets, prop it only as far as is safe.

Cut back your detergent. Use HE (high-efficiency) detergent only, and measure to the low line — with a front-loader, less is genuinely cleaner. Reduce or stop liquid fabric softener, which is a major residue source; wool dryer balls are a low-residue alternative.
Take laundry out as soon as the cycle ends instead of letting a wet load sit in the drum.
Keep it up on a schedule: run the tub-clean cycle (or a hot empty wash with cleaner) about once a month, and quickly wipe the gasket dry after heavy or frequent use.

If the musty smell is still there after a full deep-clean plus two to three weeks of the new habits, the biofilm is likely deep in the sump, drain hose, or behind the drum — book an appliance repair technician rather than repeating bleach cycles.
diyVsPro: DIY is the right call for cleaning the gasket, drawer, and drain filter and for the habit changes — that resolves the large majority of musty front-loader smells with no tools beyond a brush and gloves. Stop and call a licensed appliance repair technician if: the smell persists after a thorough clean plus a few weeks of new habits; the drum won't drain and holds standing water (a failing drain pump or blocked hose); you find heavy black mold that has spread past the gasket into the door insulation or behind the drum; or you smell a rotten-egg/sewer odor rather than a musty one — that is a drain or plumbing-vent issue, not washer mold, and belongs to a plumber. If mold has spread to a large area of the surrounding wall or floor (roughly more than 10 square feet) or there is water damage behind or under the machine, bring in a professional mold remediation service, not just an appliance tech.
typicalCostUSD: DIY: about $10-30 for washer-cleaner tablets or bleach, a brush, and gloves. Pro appliance service call: roughly $100-250 for diagnosis plus a minor part; a replacement door gasket typically runs $50-150 in parts plus labor.
timeEstimate: 30-60 minutes of hands-on cleaning, plus a tub-clean cycle of roughly 1-4 hours that runs on its own (many self-clean cycles are 2+ hours); then about 2 minutes of drying/airing habits after each wash going forward.
safetyNote: The biggest hazard here is chemical, not electrical: NEVER mix chlorine bleach with vinegar, ammonia, oxygen/percarbonate cleaners, or any other cleaner — some combinations release toxic chlorine gas. Pick one cleaner per cycle, and if you switch products, rinse the drum and surfaces thoroughly in between. Work with a window open or fan running, wear rubber gloves and eye protection when using bleach, and wear an N95 mask if you are sensitive to mold or have asthma. Before you open the drain pump filter or any access panel, unplug the washer (or switch off its breaker), let any trapped water cool if you just ran a hot cycle so it can't scald you, and keep the spilled water away from the outlet. Bleach can weaken some rubber seals and hoses over time, so follow your manufacturer's care guide on what cleaner to use. If you find mold spreading beyond the gasket into insulation or over a large area (roughly more than 10 square feet), or water damage behind or under the machine, stop and get professional remediation rather than scrubbing it yourself.
toolsParts: Old toothbrush or small detail brush
Washing-machine cleaner tablets (e.g., Affresh or Tide Washing Machine Cleaner)
Shallow pan or bowl plus old towels (for the drain filter)
Owner's manual for filter/drawer removal steps
